subject: Multiple group analyses with Likert items: some different results

messages.subject: Multiple group analyses with Likert items: some different results
parts:
Hi all,
I have found different results in the loadings step between two similar lavaan procedures (lavaan syntax vs. semTools syntax) for measurement invariance multiple group analyses. I have tried with two different bases and in each case different results were found in the loadings step.
Terrence Jorgensen and Sunthud Pornprasertmanit have tried to help me. But still I do not figure why this difference is present in the loadings step -not in the others steps. Sunthud has suggested it could be a syntax problem, but I think I have followed the lavaan web page steps (from lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html) with "group" and "group.equal" commands, and syntax from Sunthud web page (Please, see below). All the others invariance are consistent.

By example, I have used the data from www.sunthud.com/catInvariance.html example5c ["Likert items (more than 2 response outcomes)"]
This is the difference in loadings step:
semTools syntax: chisq 26.266
lavaan syntax: chisq 29.698

semTools syntax:

mIC <- measurementInvarianceCat(mymodel, data=dat5, group="g", estimator="WLSMV", parameterization="theta")

lavaan syntax:

conffit <- cfa(mymodel, data=dat5, group="g") #configural
loadfit <- cfa(mymodel, data=dat5, group="g", group.equal="loadings", parameterization="theta") #loadings
thrfit <- cfa(mymodel, data=dat5, group="g", group.equal=c("loadings", "thresholds"), parameterization="theta")#loadings+thresholds
meanfit <- cfa(mymodel, data=dat5, group="g", group.equal=c("loadings", "thresholds","means"), parameterization="theta")#loadings+thresholds+means

anova(conffit, loadfit)
anova(loadfit, thrfit)

messages.subject: Re: Multiple group analyses with Likert items: some different results
parts:
loadfit and mIC[["fit.loadings"]] have the same df, but I'm not sure that they are equivalent models (if they were, the chi-squared would be the same).  You say you read through Sunthud's lavaan scripts at the link you provided -- paying attention to those equality constraints tells you exactly how those models (and therefore, the output of measurementInvarianceCat) differ from the models you fit when you use the group.equal argument.  Your lavaan model syntax places no constraints on the thresholds whatsoever, whereas the method Sunthud (based on Millsap & Yun-Tein, 2004) does place equality constraints on the first threshold of each indicator, as well as the second threshold of the first indicator of each construct (i.e., u1 and u5) -- even in the configural model.  This enables the estimation not only of factor means in the second group, but also residual variances of each indicator's underlying latent response in the second group.  When you specify group.equal = "loadings", you did not freely estimate the residual variances, so your model-implied covariance matrix was different than the one implied by the model using semTools -- you can compare them directly:

lavInspect(loadfit, "cov.ov")
lavInspect(mIC[["fit.loadings"]], "cov.ov")

This is what makes categorical CFA so much less intuitive than CFA with continuous indicators.  The thresholds affect not only mean-structure parameters but also covariance structure parameters.  For example
  • If an indicator's latent response has a higher mean in group 2, that would manifest as a negative shift in the thresholds, but I think the distance between thresholds would stay the same (or proportionally equal, if the variances differed)
  • If an indicator's latent response has a higher variance in group 2, that would manifest as a change in the distance between thresholds
If you only have 1 threshold (binary indicator), then you cannot disentangle group-differences in means from group-differences in variances -- both would manifest as a difference in thresholds.  That is why you can't test weak and strong invariance separately with binary indicators.

Anyway, the reason you have the same df using the 2 methods is that the 8 freely estimated residual variances are compensated by the 8 equality constraints on the first thresholds, and the 2 free factor means in group 2 are compensated by the 2 additional equality constraints on the second thresholds of u1 and u5.  So the number of estimated parameters is the same, but the models are not equivalent.

And this is not a case of one method being wrong whereas the other is correct.  They are just 2 different methods, so you just need to pick one.  The Millsap & Yun-Tein (2004) method has more theoretical support because their publication was very thorough, but the point of their article was to delineate minimum identification constraints while being able to compare latent means and variances (the whole point of testing invariance).  They did not set out to make an exhaustive list of all possible ways to test measurement invariance with categorical indicators.  

Terry
